correctness.rationale: Multiplicative prime-power definitions imply p^(2^k)+1=qQ_k(p) exactly. At k=1, p-1 divides 2, giving precisely (p,q)=(2,5),(3,5). At k=2, the congruence remainder (p-1)^2+1 lies strictly between 0 and Q_k(p). At every k>=3, letting U=p^(2^(k-2)) and V=sum_(j=0)^(k-3) p^(2^j) gives Q=U^2+U+V-1, R=(U+V-1)^2+1, and U^4+1=R (mod Q). Exact expansions prove R-Q=U(2V-3)+(V-1)(V-2)+1>0 and 2Q-R=U^2-2U(V-2)-(V-2)^2>0 because U>=3(V-2), proved by induction from p^2>=3(p-2). Thus Q<R<2Q and no divisibility. A standalone script also passed 4200 prime-pair checks and 1791 modular tests; enumeration is not used for the infinite conclusion.

value.rationale: The open equality/infinitude problem motivates understanding infinite natural exponent families. The divisors of a power-of-two exponent form a pure dyadic ladder, making the family structural rather than arbitrary. The result is a complete classification for every exponent in that ladder; the prime-independent two-modulus interval eliminates infinitely many untested layers and is not a recomputation of known finite entries. The answer may inform further restrictions on candidate exponent configurations, but does not resolve global infinitude.
